```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
library(here)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(Seurat)
```

```{r load-data}
# Per-cluster summaries exported from the Seurat object by
# bts/data_generation/export_marker_explorer.R. These are small + committed, so the
# bulk of this investigation reproduces without ever loading the 91 MB object.
mex <- here("shiny", "marker-explorer")
cluster_mean    <- read_csv(file.path(mex, "cluster_mean.csv"),    show_col_types = FALSE)
cluster_pct     <- read_csv(file.path(mex, "cluster_pct.csv"),     show_col_types = FALSE)
cluster_markers <- read_csv(file.path(mex, "cluster_markers.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
gene_dict       <- read_csv(file.path(mex, "gene_dict.csv"),       show_col_types = FALSE)
umap            <- read_csv(file.path(mex, "umap_coords.csv"),     show_col_types = FALSE)

clusters <- paste0("c", 0:17)   # column names in the per-cluster matrices
```

## 1. The puzzle: 18 clusters, no labels

We finished preprocessing with a Harmony-integrated UMAP of **2,888 nuclei from four fish**
(BB48 & BB49INJ = 11-KT; BB50 & BB50INJ = vehicle) split into **18 clusters**. Clustering tells you
*which* nuclei group together — it says nothing about *what they are*. That is the annotator's job,
and for electric-organ tissue there is no off-the-shelf reference to lean on.

```{r umap-overview, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
umap <- umap |> mutate(cluster = factor(cluster, levels = 0:17))
ggplot(umap, aes(U1, U2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.8) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3), ncol = 2)) +
  labs(title = "18 Harmony clusters — but which is which?", x = "UMAP 1", y = "UMAP 2") +
  theme_classic()
```

Our **starting hypothesis**, from prior knowledge of electrocyte biology:

- **anterior face** = clusters 7 + 2
- **posterior face** = clusters 0 + 3
- **stalk** = cluster 12 or 14 (low probability 15)

anchored on `atp1b2b` and **PMCA**, which our own work shows marks the **posterior face** (not the
stalk). Spoiler: the faces hold up, but the stalk guess is wrong — and chasing *why* uncovers a whole
second axis of variation. Here's the trail.

## 2. Ground rules before touching the data

::: {.callout-important}
## Gene names are not vertebrate symbols
This is a *mormyrid* annotation. A feature's name is the gene **symbol only where one exists**, and
otherwise a `LOC########` ID. Never type a symbol from memory and assume it's present — **mine the
product descriptions and intersect with the features you actually have.** Every gene panel below is
built with this `pick()` helper, so it self-corrects to real feature names.
:::

```{r pick}
# product-description search -> features that actually exist in the matrices
pick <- function(regex) {
  intersect(gene_dict$gene[grepl(regex, gene_dict$product, ignore.case = TRUE)],
            cluster_mean$gene)
}
# mean expression of a gene set across all 18 clusters
panel_mean <- function(genes) {
  cluster_mean |> filter(gene %in% genes) |> summarise(across(all_of(clusters), mean))
}
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The PMCA decision (this overrides the teaching episode)
The annotation episode currently picks the "stalk" cluster as the one with peak PMCA × electrocyte
co-expression, citing Baumann et al. 2025 ("PMCA protein on the stalklet membrane"). But our own data
show **PMCA *transcript* is enriched in the posterior face**. Protein can traffic away from the
nucleus that made it, so protein-localization and transcript-localization need not agree.

Two cautions on how much weight PMCA can bear (see §3 for the numbers):

1. **PMCA is the *weakest* of our posterior markers.** Posterior-vs-anterior separation is only
   ~2× for PMCA, but ~6–13× for `cdh13` and ~70× for `atp1b2b`. So the face split is real, but it
   is `atp1b2b`/`cdh13` that prove it — **we treat PMCA as corroborating, not as ground truth.**
2. **Two claims, kept separate.** That there are *two distinct face programs* is solid. That the
   `atp1b2b`/`cdh13`/PMCA-high program is specifically the *posterior* face is an orientation call
   that still leans on the contested PMCA localization. We label the programs anterior/posterior
   for readability, but the *polarity* is the soft part of the story, not the existence of two faces.
:::

## 3. Reconnaissance: who's an electrocyte, and the two face programs

First, which clusters are even electrocyte-lineage? The principal electrogenic sodium channel
`scn4aa` (`LOC125742960`) is the cleanest lineage marker.

```{r lineage}
lineage <- cluster_mean |> filter(gene == "LOC125742960") |> select(all_of(clusters)) |> unlist()
electrocyte <- as.integer(gsub("c", "", names(lineage)[lineage > 2.5]))
electrocyte                       # scn4aa-high = electrocyte-lineage clusters
sort(round(lineage, 2))           # the cutoff is soft — note the borderline cases
```

The 2.5 line is eyeballed, so read it as soft: **c14 (2.70) and c11 (2.99) sit just above it**, while
**c1 (1.68) and c16 (1.85) fall just below** — c1/c16 are *not* electrocyte-lineage by this rule
(consistent with their markers; see §8 and the §10 table). Everything else is a minor non-electrocyte
population (Schwann `col28a1a` in 4/10, endothelial `cdh5` in 9, myogenic **satellite cells** in 13 —
*not* contaminating muscle; see the callout below).

::: {.callout-note}
## c13 is satellite cells, not contaminating skeletal muscle
The dissection was clean, so "muscle contamination" was always suspect. The data resolve it: c13 is the
electric organ's own **Pax7⁺ myogenic progenitor (satellite) pool**, not differentiated muscle. The
decisive logic — *contaminating fast-twitch muscle would carry the **highest** terminal-contractile
burden in the dataset and be myogenin⁺.* c13 shows the opposite on every axis.

```{r satellite, message=FALSE}
sat_cols  <- c("c13","c0","c3","c2","c7")   # satellite vs the electrocyte faces
# progenitor program: ON and population-wide (mean + % of c13 nuclei expressing)
prog <- c("pax7b","notch3","megf10","cdh15","myf5","spry1")
# terminal differentiation: OFF
term_tf <- c("myog","myf6")
left_join(
  cluster_mean |> filter(gene %in% c(prog, term_tf)) |> select(gene, all_of(sat_cols)),
  cluster_pct  |> filter(gene %in% c(prog, term_tf)) |> transmute(gene, pct_c13 = round(100*c13)),
  by = "gene")

# Contractile/sarcomere burden per cluster (61-gene panel). Satellite should be LOWER than the
# electrocytes (which are modified muscle and keep sarcomeric remnants); real muscle would be HIGHEST.
term_panel <- pick(paste0("titin|nebulin|creatine kinase M-type|myoglobin|troponin|",
                          "actin, alpha skeletal|myosin heavy|myosin, light chain|tropomyosin|sarcomeric"))
prog_panel <- pick(paste0("paired box protein Pax-?7|myogenic factor 5|",
                          "multiple epidermal growth factor-like domains 10|M-cadherin|",
                          "notch receptor 3|sprouty homolog 1"))
tibble(cluster = clusters,
       terminal_contractile = round(unlist(panel_mean(term_panel)), 2),
       progenitor           = round(unlist(panel_mean(prog_panel)), 2)) |>
  mutate(prog_over_terminal = round(progenitor / terminal_contractile, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(prog_over_terminal)) |> head(4)
```

What the two tables show:

- **Progenitor program ON, and across the whole cluster:** `pax7b` in **96%** of c13 nuclei,
  `notch3` 88%, `megf10` 69%, plus M-cadherin (`cdh15`) and `myf5`. c13 has the highest progenitor
  score of any cluster.
- **Terminal differentiation OFF:** `myog` and `myf6` are detected in **0%** of c13 nuclei.
- **Sarcomere burden *below* the electrocytes:** c13's contractile-panel mean (~0.31) is the lowest
  tier and sits under the electrocyte faces (~0.49–0.66); its progenitor/terminal ratio (~2.8) is an
  order of magnitude above every other cluster. Mature muscle would be the *highest*, not the lowest.
- **Quiescent, not proliferating:** `mki67`/`cdk1`/PCNA ≈ 0 in c13 → a resting resident pool, the
  adult-satellite (not activated-myoblast) flavour.

**The dissection vindication:** *no* cluster anywhere shows a mature-muscle profile (myogenin⁺ with
sarcomere above the electrocytes), so there is no skeletal-muscle contamination to find. c13 is the
organ's own progenitor reservoir — biologically apt, since electrocytes are muscle-derived and a
Pax7⁺ pool is what a hypertrophy-capable, 11-KT-responsive organ needs to grow.
:::

Now the face split — posterior should be `atp1b2b`/`cdh13`/PMCA-high; anterior should be low for those
and, if anything, enriched for a Kv1.7-like channel. **Note the gene-name discipline from §2:** there
is no `kcna7a` feature in the matrix — the Kv1.7-like ortholog is `LOC125743019`, which is what we use.

```{r faces}
# PMCA = LOC125738035; Kv1.7-like = LOC125743019 (NB: no "kcna7a" symbol exists here)
face_genes <- c("atp1b2b", "LOC125738035", "cdh13", "LOC125743019")
cluster_mean |> filter(gene %in% face_genes) |>
  select(gene, c0, c3, c15, c2, c7, c12, c14)
```

Clusters **0, 3 (and 15)** are `atp1b2b`/`cdh13`/PMCA-high → **posterior**; **2, 7** are low for all
three → **anterior**. The clean discriminators are `cdh13` (~6–13×) and `atp1b2b` (~70×); PMCA splits
only ~2×. The Kv1.7-like channel is *weakly* anterior-enriched (peaks at c7) — directional support, not
a strong marker, so the anterior face is mostly defined by the *absence* of the posterior program.
Before trusting any of this, rule out the boring explanation — is the split just batch (one fish)?

```{r batch-check}
# Presence isn't balance: report each cluster's largest single-fish share, not just "all 4 present".
umap |> mutate(fish = str_extract(cell, "^[^_]+")) |>
  count(cluster, fish) |>                                  # n = nuclei per (cluster, fish)
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(total          = sum(n),                       # don't shadow `n` inside summarise
            max_fish_share = round(max(n) / sum(n), 2),
            dominant_fish  = fish[which.max(n)], .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(max_fish_share))
```

The **face clusters (0/2/3/7) are well mixed** (no fish > ~42%), so the face split is **biology, not
batch**. But "all four fish present" is too weak a check on its own: several *small* clusters are
one-fish-dominated — **c8 (~50% BB48), c15 (~49% BB48), c16 (~65% BB49INJ), c17 (~55% BB50)** — which
is directly relevant to how much weight their identities can bear (see §8, §10). Two more loose ends:
clusters **12 and 14 have no coherent positive markers** (top genes detected in a handful of cells —
the hallmark of low-complexity nuclei clustering by what they *lack*), and there's a **treatment skew**
we can't yet explain — though note it is partly a *single-fish* skew (c8 is half BB48).

```{r weak-12-14}
cluster_markers |> filter(cluster %in% c(12, 14)) |>
  group_by(cluster) |> slice_max(avg_log2FC, n = 3) |>
  select(cluster, gene_name,product, avg_log2FC, pct.1, pct.2)
```

## 4. The methodological turn: predict the stalk *before* looking

Here is the mistake we almost made: "the stalk is whatever cluster is left over after I label the
faces." That's **unfalsifiable** — any leftover cluster would do.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Define a positive prediction
In mormyrids the **stalk is the innervated compartment**. So a stalk nucleus should carry the
**post-synaptic neuromuscular apparatus** — the acetylcholine-receptor subunits plus MuSK, rapsyn,
Dok7, ColQ, AChE, agrin. That's a concrete, falsifiable signature we can score. If no cluster carries
it, we haven't found the stalk — and that's an honest result, not a failure.
:::

```{r nmj-panel}
nmj_panel <- pick(paste0(
  "cholinergic receptor, nicotinic|rapsyn|receptor-associated protein of the synapse|",
  "docking protein 7|muscle.*receptor tyrosine kinase|acetylcholinesterase|",
  "collagen-like tail|agrin"))
nmj_panel
```

## 5. The redirect: scoring the innervation module

Average the innervation panel across clusters. If our hypothesis (stalk = 12/14) is right, 12 or 14
should top this.

```{r nmj-rank}
round(sort(unlist(panel_mean(nmj_panel)), decreasing = TRUE), 3)
```

**It isn't 12 or 14 — it's cluster 17**, and 12/14 sit near the bottom. The per-nucleus module score
(below; needs the object, so it's `eval=FALSE` with a pre-generated figure) tells the same story even
more cleanly:

```{r modulescore-object, eval=FALSE}
# --- needs the Seurat object; figure produced by make_figures.R ---
s <- readRDS(here("episodes/data/checkpoints/02_harmony_clustered.rds"))
s <- AddModuleScore(s, features = list(Stalk = nmj_panel), name = "Stalk", nbin = 12, ctrl = 50)
VlnPlot(s, "Stalk1", group.by = "seurat_clusters", pt.size = 0)
FeaturePlot(s, "Stalk1", reduction = "umap.harmony", order = TRUE)
```
The clincher is a single gene: **MuSK**, the master organizer of the post-synaptic membrane. It is
specific to cluster 17 and essentially absent elsewhere.

```{r musk}
cluster_mean |> filter(gene %in% c("musk", "chrnb1", "chrna1", "chrne")) |>
  select(gene, c17, c5, c6, c8, c0, c7)
```

```{r musk-object, eval=FALSE}
# figure from make_figures.R
FeaturePlot(s, c("musk", "chrnb1", "chrna1", "chrne"), reduction = "umap.harmony", order = TRUE)
```

And what about 12/14? Their UMAP centroids sit *between* the anterior and posterior faces — a
face-to-face transition, not a separate compartment — while clusters **5, 6, 8, 17 form their own
island** far from every face cluster:

```{r centroids}
umap |> mutate(cluster = as.integer(as.character(cluster))) |>
  group_by(cluster) |> summarise(U1 = round(mean(U1), 1), U2 = round(mean(U2), 1), n = n()) |>
  filter(cluster %in% c(0, 3, 15, 2, 7, 12, 14, 5, 6, 8, 17))
```

So the stalk hypothesis was **half right and half wrong**: faces 7/2 and 0/3 hold, but the stalk is
the **5/6/8/17 island** (anchored by c17), and 12/14 are inter-face transitional nuclei.

## 6. An expert's caution reshapes the model

Cluster 17 is not "the stalk" — it's the **NMJ region** of the stalk. Mormyrid stalks have three
anatomical zones, and only the synaptic one should carry the MuSK/AChR signature:

::: {.callout-note}
## Three stalk compartments
1. **NMJ region** — compact nuclei apposed to the motorneuron + myelin (the synapse).
2. **Stalk proper** — the trunk, with no neurons on it.
3. **Microstalklets** — profusely branching membrane after the stalk penetrates the electrocyte.

This is the electrocyte version of **subsynaptic (sole-plate) nuclei** in skeletal muscle: in a
multinucleate syncytium, the few nuclei under the synapse run a different program (Agrin→LRP4→MuSK→
AChR) from the rest. Cluster 17 = those subsynaptic nuclei.
:::

![Electrocyte anatomy: anterior/posterior faces and the penetrating, innervated stalk system. *(Add source citation.)*](cluster_sleuthing/figures/electrocyte_anatomy.png)

::: {.callout-note}
## "Where are the motorneurons?" — a consistency check, not a gap
We annotate the *post-synaptic* side of the synapse (c17) but there is no motorneuron cluster. That is
exactly right, and it's worth saying why, because it's a clean lesson in what a tissue dissection can
and can't contain.

**The reason is anatomy, not the snRNA-vs-scRNA distinction.** A motorneuron's soma — and therefore its
**nucleus and essentially all its mRNA** — sits in the spinal cord/hindbrain; only the distal **axon
terminal** reaches the organ to innervate the stalk. So the motorneuron cell body simply *isn't in the
EO sample*. Single-**cell** of this tissue would miss them too — you can't dissociate a cell body that
isn't there. The genuine single-nucleus blind spot applies only to the one piece that *is* physically
present, the anucleate axon terminal (with its locally-translated mRNA): snRNA-seq sees only nuclei, so
it can't read a bouton — though scRNA-seq wouldn't recover it as a clean "motorneuron" either.

The data bear this out — the entire cholinergic-motorneuron module is flat:

```{r motorneuron}
mn <- list(
  ChAT  = pick("choline O-acetyltransferase|choline acetyltransferase"),
  VAChT = pick("solute carrier family 18 member A3|vesicular acetylcholine"),
  MNX1  = pick("motor neuron and pancreas homeobox|homeobox HB9"),
  ISL1  = pick("insulin gene enhancer protein ISL"),
  MAP2  = pick("microtubule-associated protein 2\\b"))
sapply(mn, function(g) if (length(g)) round(max(unlist(panel_mean(g))), 3) else NA)  # peak across all clusters
```

What we *do* capture is anatomically consistent: the **post-synaptic** nuclei (c17, MuSK/AChR) and the
axon's **glial escort** (Schwann cells, c4/c10, which are resident in the organ and ensheath the
intra-organ axon). The neuron's own nucleus is the only missing piece — precisely what anatomy
predicts, so its absence *corroborates* the c17 = NMJ call rather than undercutting it.
:::

## 7. Resolving the island into zones

If the island is the stalk, its three zones should be visible inside it. What unifies the island
versus the faces?

```{r island-diff}
isl <- c("c5", "c6", "c8", "c17"); fc <- c("c0", "c2", "c3", "c7", "c15")
cluster_mean |>
  mutate(island = rowMeans(across(all_of(isl))),
         face   = rowMeans(across(all_of(fc))),
         d      = island - face) |>
  filter(island > 0.5) |> slice_max(d, n = 12) |>
  left_join(gene_dict, by = "gene") |>
  transmute(gene, island = round(island, 2), face = round(face, 2), d = round(d, 2),
            product = substr(product, 1, 44))
```

The island signature is **membrane-cytoskeleton + axon-guidance**: utrophin, β-spectrin, plectin,
Slit2/Robo2 — exactly what an elaborate branching stalk membrane needs. Splitting by zone marker:

```{r zones}
zone_genes <- c("musk", "chrnb1", "utrn",      # NMJ / subsynaptic
                "robo2", "slit2",              # microstalklets (branching)
                "sptb", "LOC125719088",        # stalk proper (spectrin, plectin)
                "LOC125721913", "ndufa4a")     # ribo/OXPHOS axis (contested; see §8)
cluster_mean |> filter(gene %in% zone_genes) |> select(gene, c17, c5, c6, c8)
```

- **c17 → NMJ**: MuSK, AChR-β1, utrophin peak. This is the firm call.
- **c5 / c6 → two stalk-*body* programs**, *tentatively* microstalklets vs stalk-proper. Be honest
  about the limit here: the **only** marker that cleanly separates them is `robo2` (c5 = 2.96 vs
  c6 = 1.19). `slit2` is essentially equal (3.82 vs 3.67) and β-spectrin (`sptb`) is actually
  *higher* in c6 (2.73 vs 2.14) — so the specific zone labels are a reasonable guess, not a
  marker-discriminated result. And the 4-clusters → 4-zones correspondence is partly an artifact of
  clustering resolution (a different resolution could give 3 or 5 island clusters), so don't read it
  as "cluster count = zone count."
- **c8 → not a zone**: ribosomal/OXPHOS-dominated housekeeping with no compartment program — see §8
  (the preprocessing episode flags it as a contamination cluster).

::: {.callout-warning}
## MEF2 is a lineage marker, not a stalk marker
A MEF2A-like gene (`LOC125705937`) tops the island-vs-face list — tempting to call it a stalk marker.
But **`mef2aa` characterizes electrocyte nuclei generally (and muscle nuclei too)**
([Gallant et al. 2012, *J Exp Biol* 215:2479](https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/215/14/2479)).
It marks the *myogenic lineage*, not a compartment, so we do **not** use it to define the stalk.
(Open question: why is it ~5× higher in the island than the faces if it's pan-electrocyte? Possibly a
distinct paralog, or simply that island nuclei are more transcriptionally active than the quieter,
terminally specialized face nuclei.)
:::

The four island clusters already *are* the four zones — so we just need to see them side by side,
grouped by their original identities.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Gotcha: `subset()` + `FindClusters()` renumbers clusters from 0
A tempting move is to re-cluster the island (`subset()` then `FindNeighbors()` → `FindClusters()`).
But re-running `FindClusters()` clusters those cells *afresh* and overwrites `seurat_clusters` with
**new IDs starting at 0** — they have nothing to do with the original 5/6/8/17, which is why a DotPlot
grouped by `seurat_clusters` then shows a mysterious "0–7" on the axis. `subset()` on its own *keeps*
the parent identities, so the fix is to group by those (stash them first if you do re-cluster):
:::

```{r island-zones-object, eval=FALSE}
# figure from make_figures.R. subset() KEEPS the parent identities (5/6/8/17);
# we group by those so the y-axis stays interpretable. (No re-clustering needed —
# re-running FindClusters() here would renumber the subset from 0.)
isl <- subset(s, idents = c(5, 6, 8, 17))
isl$island_cluster <- factor(as.character(Idents(isl)), levels = c("17", "5", "6", "8"))
DotPlot(isl, group.by = "island_cluster", features = zone_genes) + RotatedAxis()
```

![The four island clusters vs zone markers: 17 = NMJ (MuSK/AChR/utrophin), 5 = microstalklets (Slit2/Robo2), 6 = stalk-proper (spectrin/plectin); 8 is dominated by ribosomal/OXPHOS housekeeping rather than a zone program (contested — see §8).](cluster_sleuthing/figures/07_island_zone_dotplot.png)

## 8. The mystery clusters 12 / 14 / 15 — and a second axis

We deferred 12/14/15. Which clusters do they actually resemble? Correlate every cluster's expression
profile (on the 2,000 most variable genes) and read off nearest neighbors:

```{r nearest}
v  <- cluster_mean |> mutate(.v = apply(across(all_of(clusters)), 1, var)) |> slice_max(.v, n = 2000)
cc <- cor(as.matrix(v[, clusters]))
sapply(c("c12", "c14", "c15"),
       function(q) names(sort(cc[q, setdiff(clusters, q)], decreasing = TRUE))[1:3])
```

`15` is a near-twin of the posterior face (0/3); `12` and `14` track the anterior face (2). And
they're **not doublets** — each is overwhelmingly electrocyte, with no second cell type:

```{r doublet}
mods <- list(Electrocyte = c("LOC125742960", "atp1b2b"),
             Muscle      = c("pax7b", "myom2a"),
             Schwann     = c("col28a1a", "smoc1"),
             Endothelial = c("cdh5", "pecam1b"))
sapply(mods, function(g)
  cluster_mean |> filter(gene %in% g) |> summarise(across(c(c12, c14, c15), mean)) |>
    round(2) |> unlist())
```

So why do they form separate clusters at all? Because a **second axis** cuts across compartment: a
coordinated **ribosomal + mitochondrial-transcript** signal, concentrated in exactly **c8, c15, c14**
— the same clusters that are 11-KT-skewed. Ribosomal fraction: **c8 ≈ 9.2%, c15 ≈ 3.2%, c14 ≈ 1.9%,
all others < 1%** (object metadata; figure below). *What that axis means is genuinely contested* —
see the debate below.

```{r qc-object, eval=FALSE}
# figures from make_figures.R. The object already carries `percent_ribo` from preprocessing.
# nFeature_RNA / nCount_RNA per cluster is the key control for the "intermediate / under-characterized"
# clusters (12/14/15/1/16): if those are simply low-complexity nuclei, they will sit low here, and the
# "transition state" reading loses ground to "sparse nuclei clustering by what they lack."
VlnPlot(s, c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent_ribo"),
        group.by = "seurat_clusters", pt.size = 0)
ox <- pick("NADH:ubiquinone|cytochrome c oxidase subunit|ATP synthase membrane")
s  <- AddModuleScore(s, list(OxPhos = ox), name = "OxPhos", nbin = 12, ctrl = 50)
VlnPlot(s, "OxPhos1", group.by = "seurat_clusters", pt.size = 0)
```

![QC per cluster — ribosomal fraction spikes in c8/c15/c14.](cluster_sleuthing/figures/08_qc_violin.png)

![Mitochondrial-biogenesis (OXPHOS) module — the same clusters.](cluster_sleuthing/figures/08_oxphos_violin.png)

::: {.callout-warning}
## What is this second axis — biology or contamination? (unresolved)
This is the hardest call in the whole investigation, and it is **not settled by this dataset**. Two
readings compete:

**Reading A — ambient/cytoplasmic contamination** (the preprocessing episode's position; see its
"Ribosomal content flags a contamination cluster" section). Ribosomal-protein mRNAs are *cytoplasmic*;
a clean nuclear prep should be depleted of them, so a cluster *defined* by ribosomal load is the
classic signature of cytoplasmic carryover / ambient soup — especially in mitochondria- and
ribosome-rich electric organ. **c8 (≈9%) fits this squarely**: it's a categorical outlier with no
coherent cell-type program (its "markers" are *only* ribosomal + OXPHOS housekeeping).

**Reading B — a hormone-driven anabolic state.** 11-KT enlarges electrocytes and lengthens the EOD —
growth that demands more ribosomes (protein synthesis) and more mitochondria (ion pumping). On this
view c8/c15/c14 are the activated states of their compartments, and the 11-KT skew is the cause.

**Reading C — a per-sample technical artifact.** The "82% 11-KT" enrichment of c8 is, more precisely,
**50% one fish (BB48: 76/153 nuclei)**. A cluster that is half a single animal is the fingerprint of
a per-prep effect (one dissociation with more cytoplasmic carryover), which is distinct from both
"ambient in general" and "hormone biology." This *strengthens* the c8 = contamination call, but it
also means the treatment framing is partly a single-animal effect.

**The design ceiling (why this can't be fully settled here).** With **2 fish per group**, treatment,
individual, and prep-batch are mutually confounded — readings A, B, and C cannot be separated even in
principle from this dataset. The tests proposed below *narrow* the question; they do not settle it.

**A correction worth flagging.** An earlier draft argued the OXPHOS markers being *nuclear-encoded*
made the signal "genuine, not ambient." *That reasoning is wrong.* Nuclear-encoded only rules out
*mtDNA* ambient RNA; ribosomal-protein and nuclear-encoded OXPHOS mRNAs are themselves cytoplasmic and
abundant in the ambient soup, so "nuclear-encoded" does **not** distinguish biology from contamination.
The 82%-11-KT skew doesn't settle it either: hypertrophic 11-KT tissue has more ribosome/mito-rich
cytoplasm, so its ambient soup — and any carryover — is richer too. Contamination predicts the same skew.

**Where it actually lands.** For **c8** the evidence favors **contamination** (9% outlier, no program
beyond housekeeping). For **c14/c15** it's genuinely open: their ribo is *mild* (1.9% / 3.2%) and they
carry **real compartment identity** (15 → posterior, 14 → anterior, from the correlation above, which
is independent of the ribo axis), so a faint biological signal and low-level carryover are
indistinguishable here. **What would break the tie:** the spliced/unspliced (intronic) ratio — genuine
*nuclear transcription* shows unspliced reads, ambient cytoplasmic mRNA is mature/spliced; a coherent
program in c14/c15 *beyond* ribo/mito; or a within-compartment 11-KT-vs-vehicle test after regressing
the ribosomal axis out.
:::

## 9. Reading marker tables honestly (the lesson hiding in the numbers)

Students get tripped up reconciling `avg_log2FC` with percent-expressed. `robo2` looks like a perfect
marker (91% of cells); `musk` is in only ~36% of cluster-17 nuclei yet we leaned on it heavily. Are
these three orthogonal numbers?

```{r specificity}
sizes <- umap |> count(cluster) |> transmute(cl = paste0("c", cluster), n) |> tibble::deframe()
pct_in  <- function(g, cl) cluster_pct[[cl]][cluster_pct$gene == g]
pct_out <- function(g, cl) {
  others <- setdiff(clusters, cl)
  sum(sapply(others, function(c) cluster_pct[[c]][cluster_pct$gene == g] * sizes[c])) / sum(sizes[others])
}
tibble(gene    = c("robo2", "musk", "chrnb1", "utrn", "scn4aa"),
       feature = c("robo2", "musk", "chrnb1", "utrn", "LOC125742960"),
       cluster = c("c5", "c17", "c17", "c17", "c17")) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(`pct.1 (%)` = round(100 * pct_in(feature, cluster)),
         `pct.2 (%)` = round(100 * pct_out(feature, cluster)),
         specificity = round(`pct.1 (%)` / pmax(`pct.2 (%)`, 0.5), 1)) |>
  ungroup() |> select(-feature)
```

The key: **marker quality is the *gap* between pct.1 and pct.2, not pct.1 alone.** By that measure
`musk` (36% vs ~4%) is *more* specific to c17 than `robo2` is to c5 — it's just detected in fewer
nuclei. `scn4aa` at ~98% looks great until you see pct.2 ≈ 83%: it labels "electrocyte," not a
cluster.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why a real marker shows up in only a third of cells
**Dropout, and it scales with expression level.** snRNA-seq is a shallow snapshot, so low-abundance
transcripts read as zero in many nuclei even when truly on. `musk` (mean 0.41) is a low-copy signaling
receptor; `robo2` (mean ~3) is ~7× more abundant and so detected nearly everywhere. *Analogy:* a
short camera exposure of the night sky — bright stars appear in every frame, dim stars flicker in and
out though they're always there. **Fix for sparse markers: pool several into a module score**
(`AddModuleScore`) — each drops out in different nuclei, so the combined score recovers the population
no single gene captures. That's exactly why §5 scored the whole NMJ panel instead of trusting `musk`
alone.
:::

## 10. Where we landed

The investigation reframes the map as **two axes** — a solid anatomical-compartment axis, and a
ribosomal/mitochondrial-transcript axis **whose meaning (ambient contamination vs hormone-driven
anabolic state) is unresolved** (§8):

| Cluster(s) | Identity | Anchor evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 3 | Posterior face | `atp1b2b`, PMCA, `cdh13` high |
| 15 | Posterior face + mild ribo elevation *(contested)* | correlates with 0/3; ribo ≈ 3.2% |
| 2, 7 | Anterior face | `atp1b2b`/`cdh13`/PMCA-low; Kv1.7-like (`LOC125743019`) weakly higher |
| 14 | Anterior face + mild ribo elevation *(contested)* | correlates with 2; ribo ≈ 1.9% |
| 12 | Anterior intermediate (vehicle) | correlates with 2; ribo low |
| 17 | **Stalk — NMJ / subsynaptic** (n = 44; MuSK⁺ in ~16) | MuSK (unique), AChR, utrophin peak |
| 5 | **Stalk — body program** (tentatively microstalklets) | `robo2` in 91% (the only marker separating it from c6); `slit2` high but ~equal in c6 |
| 6 | **Stalk — body program** (tentatively stalk-proper) | β-spectrin/plectin (membrane skeleton); zone vs c5 not strongly discriminated |
| 8 | Ribosomal/OXPHOS-dominated — **likely contamination** (see preprocessing) | ribo ≈ 9.2% outlier; no cell-type program; ~50% one fish |
| 4, 10 / 9 | Schwann / endothelial | `col28a1a`+`smoc1` / `cdh5`+`pecam1b` |
| 13 | **Myogenic satellite cells** (not contaminating muscle) | `pax7b` 96%, `notch3`, `megf10`, M-cadherin; `myog`/`myf6` = 0; sarcomere *below* electrocytes (§3 callout) |
| 16 | **Immune / myeloid** (not electrocyte; below `scn4aa` cutoff) | `dok2`, IL-8-like, CCR8-like, C1q-receptor; `scn4aa` 1.85 |
| 1 | Non-electrocyte / progenitor-like (below `scn4aa` cutoff) | prominin-1 (CD133), ST18, shisa-6; `scn4aa` 1.68 |
| 11 | Under-characterized electrocyte state | open (homeobox TFs + `myl2a`) |

**What would clinch it:** the strongest confirmations are *spatial*, not more single-cell reanalysis.
For an anatomical-compartment claim in a non-model organism the gold standard is **RNAscope / in-situ
hybridization of `musk` (and `atp1b2b`/`cdh13`) on electric-organ sections** — that converts "c17
looks like NMJ nuclei" into "MuSK transcript localizes to the innervated zone," and would also pin the
anterior/posterior polarity that PMCA alone leaves contested. Internal corroborations woven in above:
the MuSK/AChR FeaturePlot localizing to c17 (§5) and the island subclustering into zone signatures
(§7). For the contested ribosomal axis (§8): the **spliced/unspliced (intronic) ratio** (nuclear
transcription vs mature ambient mRNA), whether c14/c15 carry any coherent program *beyond* ribo/mito,
and a within-compartment 11-KT-vs-vehicle test after regressing the ribosomal axis out — but with
**n = 2 fish per group, none of these can fully separate biology from artifact** (§8).

**Implications for the teaching episode:** drop PMCA-as-stalk-marker (it's enriched in the posterior
face, though `atp1b2b`/`cdh13` are the cleaner anchors); relabel 15 → posterior; set stalk = the
5/6/17 island zones with c17 as the firm NMJ zone (5/6 as two stalk-body programs, zone labels
tentative); treat c8 as the ribosomal-contamination cluster the preprocessing episode already flags;
and relabel c16 → immune/myeloid (it is not electrocyte-lineage). The durable story —
electrocytes as modified syncytial muscle with subsynaptic-nucleus specialization — is a clean
illustration of why a cluster can mean a **compartment**, a **state**, *or a technical artifact*, and
why telling the last two apart is genuinely hard.
